summary: Three.js is an open source JavaScript library for drawing three-dimensional scenes in a web browser. Its core covers drawing and scene structure: a scene tree, cameras, materials, lights and shadows, skinning, morph targets, instancing, keyframe animation, positioned sound through the browser's own audio engine, and an immersive session manager that drives WebXR. Almost everything else people associate with the library sits in the addons folder of the same repository as optional modules rather than in the core build: every file format reader and writer including glTF, USD and FBX, all post-processing on the WebGL path, the camera controls, and thin wrappers around three outside physics engines that are fetched from a content delivery network at run time. There is no networking of any kind, no avatar format or skeleton agreement, no identity, rights or provenance model, and no geospatial frame. Two traps for a standards audience: the WebGL renderer is still the default import and the WebGPU renderer is a separate entry point, and a growing set of newer features (Gaussian splats, MaterialX materials) runs only on the WebGPU path. A third: the whole Gaussian splat stack is on the development branch and is in no tagged release up to r185, so a claim that Three.js renders splats is true of the branch and not of the shipped library.

coverage.note: Core ships two complete renderers: WebGLRenderer with its own render lists, sorting and shadow pass, and WebGPURenderer built on a render pipeline, render context and render bundle layer in src/renderers/common.

coverage.note: Point clouds are core (Points and PointsMaterial) and three-dimensional textures are supported, with point cloud readers for pcd, vox, xyz and medical volume files as addons; what is missing is any volumetric video path or compressed point cloud codec.

Core has no text at all; addons give extruded text geometry from the project's own font format plus a font reader, a font converter for TrueType, a small canvas-texture label class for immersive use, and DOM-based label renderers, but no signed distance field text and no text layout.
Perspective, orthographic, stereo, cube and array cameras are core, the last of these being what the immersive session manager fills with one view per eye; every camera control scheme is an addon.
A single Object3D tree with parent and child links, world matrix propagation, visibility, render layers and traversal is the centre of the library.

The up axis is positive Y by default and a camera looks along its own negative Z, the right-handed arrangement glTF also uses; rotations are quaternions with Euler order XYZ by default, and four-by-four matrices are stored column-major even though the setter takes its arguments in reading order, which is a common source of transcription errors.

coverage.note: Core only reads and writes the project's own JSON scene format through ObjectLoader and toJSON; every interchange container is an addon, and read and write support is lopsided: glTF, USD including USDZ, OBJ, PLY and STL both ways, while FBX, Collada, VRML, 3MF, AMF, 3DM, LDraw, LWO and VOX are read only.

Core encodes meshes as typed-array attribute buffers with optional interleaving and indices and can serialise them; what is missing is any compression in core, so Draco, mesh optimiser compression and quantised attributes all arrive only through addon readers, and the glTF writer cannot write any of them back.

coverage.note: The library draws one client's scene and has no multi-user model at all: no replication, no authority, no interest management and no prediction anywhere in the core or addon trees.
The only network use is fetching asset files over HTTP through the file loader; there is no session wire protocol of any kind.
There is no world to join, so no joining, authentication or roster concept exists; the word session in this project means an immersive device session, not a shared one.
Video arrives as a browser video element or media stream wrapped in a video texture, and audio the same way; the delivery of those streams is entirely the browser's and the application's business.
Core has a clock and a timer for local frame timing only; there is no shared or agreed time base, because there is nothing to share it with.
Nothing in the project touches identity, credentials, permission grants, selective disclosure, reputation or rights enforcement.

Coordinates are plain scene coordinates with no Earth frame; there is no geodetic position, no coordinate reference system handling and no globe, which is where a geospatial library such as CesiumJS differs.

Core surfaces the device's plane detection as an event and supports depth sensing, and an addon turns detected planes into meshes; what is missing is anchors and hit testing, which are never wrapped, so the augmented reality examples call the browser's own hit test interface directly using the reference space the renderer exposes.

coverage.note: No persistent or shared anchor handling, and no way to store or exchange one, which follows from having no networking.
Nothing in the project reads or streams a tile set; the addon readers all take a single whole file.

Immersive sessions are core on both renderers: an XR manager on renderer.xr owns the session, requests a reference space that defaults to floor level, drives an array camera with one view per eye, sets foveation, uses a projection layer where the device supports layers and a plain graphics layer otherwise, and handles depth sensing; only the buttons that start a session are addons.

coverage.note: Every reader parses whatever bytes it is given inside the page's own origin, with no isolation and no limits, so the only boundary around untrusted content is the browser's rather than the library's.
No memory, time or draw call budget for guest content; the renderer reports counts after the fact through its info object but enforces nothing.
There is no running world to persist; a scene can be written to the project's own JSON and read back, which is a file, not world state.
Assets are always referred to by path or URL; nothing hashes content or resolves a hash, and the loading cache is keyed by URL.

The library ships as an npm package with module entry points for core, addons, the WebGPU build and the shading language, but it defines no package format for a runnable experience; an application is an HTML page the author assembles.
